title: Dr Ambedkar and the working class
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Ahead of Ambedkar Jayanti: his Independent Labour Party, his years as Labour Member (1942-46), the Directive Principles and his link with Thengadi Ji.
body:
**Dr Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar** (1891–1956) is remembered above all as the chief architect of the Constitution of India. Ahead of Ambedkar Jayanti on 14 April, it is worth recalling a part of his life that is less often discussed: his work as a thinker, organiser and lawmaker on questions of labour. Workers' wages, hours of work, insurance, union recognition and the right to strike were all subjects on which he spoke, wrote and legislated. His life also touches the story of the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh through the person of its founder, Dattopant Thengadi.

## Early engagement with workers

Ambedkar's concern with labour began in Bombay's mill districts. Accounts of the 1928 textile strike record that he pressed for workers from the so-called lower castes to be given access to all mill jobs, a demand that had to be included in the strikers' charter. For him, the labour question and the caste question could not be separated. He once described caste as a division of labourers, not merely a division of labour. That phrase, preserved in several accounts of his thought, explains why he saw equality at the workplace and equality in society as two sides of the same demand.

## The Independent Labour Party

In **August 1936** he founded the **Independent Labour Party** (ILP). Its programme was addressed to the labouring classes, in particular the landless, tenants and industrial workers. It promised public works and resettlement for the unemployed and landless, laws to protect peasants from moneylenders, cooperatives and land mortgage banks, and, where necessary, state ownership and management of industry. In the 1937 provincial elections, the first held under the Government of India Act, 1935, the party contested 17 seats in the Bombay Legislative Assembly and won nearly all of them; accounts differ slightly on whether the number was 14 or 15.

The ILP's most important labour battle came in 1938, when the Bombay government introduced an Industrial Disputes Bill that made conciliation compulsory and penalised illegal strikes. Ambedkar opposed it in the Assembly, calling it the "Workers' Civil Liberties Suspension Act", and argued that punishing workers for striking would amount to making the worker a slave. A one-day strike in the textile mills on 15 November 1938 was held against the Bill. The right to strike, in his words as reported, was part of the right to freedom.

## Labour Member, 1942 to 1946

From **1942 to 1946** Ambedkar served as the **Labour Member** in the Viceroy's Executive Council, in effect India's labour minister at the time. Several accounts note that he was appointed in July 1942, and that he left when the Council was reconstituted in August 1946.

Those years were the years of the Second World War, and labour issues multiplied: wartime production, rising prices, shortages of food. Among the measures and initiatives associated with his tenure in the sources are these:

- **Tripartism.** On 7 August 1942, at the fourth Tripartite National Labour Conference in New Delhi, he stressed uniform labour legislation across provinces. Employers' and workers' representatives were brought to the same table with the Government, a practice that later developed into the Indian Labour Conference.
- **Working hours.** He is associated with the push for an eight-hour working day, and with amendments to the Factories Act that set a 48-hour week, required washing facilities, and gave paid holidays to workers with twelve months of continuous service.
- **Social insurance.** He is credited with drafting the legislation that became the **Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948**, covering medical care and other benefits, and with framing a provident fund and bonus scheme for coal mines.
- **Women workers.** Accounts credit him with maternity benefit measures in mines, creches and pithead baths, and with arguing for equal pay for equal work regardless of sex.
- **Union recognition.** In November 1943 he moved the Indian Trade Unions (Amendment) Bill to make recognition of unions by employers compulsory.
- **Employment exchanges and wages.** He is associated with the first employment exchanges to match workers to jobs and with groundwork for what became the Minimum Wages Act, 1948. On the Payment of Wages (Amendment) Bill, he argued against different payment deadlines for large and small factories and proposed a uniform deadline of seven days. Readers will notice that the principle of a seven-day deadline for monthly wages appears in the Code on Wages of today.
- **Field visits.** He visited the Dhanbad coalfields in December 1943 and the Koderma mica mines in 1944, inspecting mines, housing and a school for miners' children, and said that without adequate wages no reform would be possible.

Historians may differ on the details and on how much credit belongs to him personally and how much to the departments and the circumstances of the time, but the direction of his work is clear: labour was to be treated as a partner in production, not as a commodity.

## The Constitution and the working class

Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly. The labour-related provisions of the Constitution are mostly in the Directive Principles of State Policy. Article 38 asks the State to minimise inequalities of income and status. Article 39 asks for adequate livelihood for men and women, equal pay for equal work, and protection of the health and strength of workers. Article 41 speaks of work and public assistance in unemployment, old age and sickness; Article 42, of just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief; Article 43, of a living wage and decent conditions of work; and Article 43A, of the participation of workers in management. Under Article 37 these principles are not enforceable by courts but are fundamental in the governance of the country, and the Labour Codes of today are, in a sense, part of an effort to give them effect.

In his concluding speech to the Constituent Assembly on 25 November 1949, he warned that from 26 January 1950 the country would enter a life of contradictions. In politics there would be equality, with every citizen having a vote of equal value. In social and economic life, inequality would persist. He cautioned that if the contradiction were not removed soon, those who suffered inequality would blow up the structure of political democracy the Assembly had built. He also spoke of fraternity, without which equality and liberty would be only coats of paint.

## Thengadi Ji and Ambedkar

BMS's founder, Dattopant Thengadi, was born on 10 November 1920 at Arvi in Wardha district and founded the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh on 23 July 1955 at Bhopal. In a 2019 article based on Thengadi Ji's own recollections, published in *Organiser*, he is described as having worked closely with Dr Ambedkar between 1952 and 1956, and as having served as general secretary of the Scheduled Castes Federation. That account is Thengadi Ji's own recollection, and readers should treat it as such. It also records how, in the 1954 Bhandara by-election, Ambedkar objected to a plan that would have cost him votes, and how Thengadi Ji later recalled a conversation just before Ambedkar's conversion to Buddhism in 1956.

Thengadi Ji later wrote a book on Ambedkar, *Dr. Ambedkar aur Samajik Kranti ki Yatra*, which is listed on the Thengadi archive website, and the same archive records that he founded the **Samajik Samrasata Manch**, among other organisations. These associations help explain why BMS speaks of social harmony as a part of its labour philosophy: the idea that a worker's dignity cannot be secured if the society around him is divided by caste.

## The common thread

For both Ambedkar and Thengadi, the dignity of labour was inseparable from social equality. Ambedkar's life reminds every union of three things. First, a union must defend the weakest worker, whatever his caste or sector. Second, the right to organise and to bargain, and even the right to strike, is part of a worker's freedom. Third, rights in the statute book are not enough without fraternity on the shop floor. For any union, that is not a theory but a daily test.
